name: Bedchamber
description: A room with a bed in it that is also used for other things. Until roughly 1840 the Anglo-American chamber was not a room reserved for sleeping: people sat in it, worked in it, received callers in it, gave birth and died in it, and the best chamber was frequently the best-furnished room in the house and frequently on the ground floor. The bed itself - a full tester with hangings - is the most valuable single object in a majority of eighteenth-century probate inventories, often worth more than everything else in the room together, and it was there to be seen. Understanding this is what makes eighteenth-century plans legible: a ground-floor chamber opening off the parlour is not a compromise or a sick room, it is the normal arrangement, and the modern main-floor primary suite is a return to it rather than an invention.

history.note: The chamber becomes the bedroom over about forty years in the middle of the nineteenth century, and three things drive it. The bed gets cheap: iron bedsteads and the machine-made mattress remove the bed from the display economy, and by 1870 a bed is furniture rather than treasure. The household separates into zones: the Victorian project of a public floor and a private floor puts every bed upstairs and makes a ground-floor bed a sign of illness or of servants. And the room loses its other functions one at a time - the birth moves to the hospital between 1900 and 1940, the death follows it, and the sitting moves to the parlour. What is left is a room for sleeping, which is what a bedroom is. The catalogue keeps both entries because a plan that puts a chamber where a bedroom belongs, or the reverse, reads wrong for reasons the designer usually cannot name.

dimensions.critical_dimension: THE BED PLUS THE SITTING. A chamber is a bedroom that also holds two chairs and a small table with 30 in of clear floor round them, and that is what makes it 14 by 17 rather than 11 by 12. The tester bed is the other half: a full-tester bedstead is 60 to 66 in wide, 78 to 84 long and 84 to 96 TALL to the top of the tester, so it needs a ceiling of 9 ft to stand under and it must not be placed under a sloping ceiling or a low beam. A chamber with a 7 ft 6 in ceiling cannot take the bed the room was designed around, and a reproduction that puts a tester bed in an 8 ft room has produced a piece of furniture touching the cornice.

furniture.note: Height 84-96 in to the tester. The hangings are the point: a curtained bed is a room within a room, and it is how privacy was obtained in a house where the chamber was not private.

furniture.item: clothes press or chest of drawers
pair of side chairs and a small table
furniture.note: The chairs are what make it a chamber. A room with a bed and no seating is a bedroom.
Basin and ewer. The chamber's plumbing until about 1890, and the reason chamber floors were often painted or oilclothed near it.

A chamber hearth opening is 30-36 in wide against a parlour's 36-48. A heated chamber and an unheated one are different rooms socially, and the chimney count on the elevation tells you how many of each the house had.

daylight.orientation: East for the morning, and in an unheated house a south or east chamber was materially warmer than a north one - which is why in a five-bay Georgian the best chamber is over the parlour and on the sunny end, and why the north-east chamber is the one the children got.
daylight.note: Two sides lit where the plan allows, because a corner chamber is cross-ventilated and, before mechanical cooling, cross-ventilation is what made an upper room sleepable in July. In a single-pile plan every chamber is a corner chamber, and that is the largest single reason the type survived in the South a century after the North abandoned it.

must_adjoin.why: A chamber is entered from the passage or from the stair. In the eighteenth century it could also legitimately be entered THROUGH another chamber - the enfilade of chambers is ordinary in period plans and the modern prohibition on through-bedrooms is a modern rule. Say so rather than reproducing a period plan and then apologising for it.
exceptions: hall-and-parlor and center-passage-single-pile plans, where chamber-through-chamber circulation is the type

should_adjoin.why: The apartment sequence. Where the house is large enough, chamber and dressing room are one unit.

must_not_adjoin.why: Heat, smell and noise, and in a period house the fire risk. A chamber over a kitchen is the hottest room in the house in August.
exceptions: Small vernacular types - hall-single-cell, double-pen, shotgun - where there is no alternative and the bed is in the room with the fire.

servicing.ventilation: Cross-ventilation from two walls, and an operable transom over the passage door where the chamber is in a double-pile plan - the transom is not decoration, it is the device that made the back chamber habitable, and removing it in a renovation is why so many restored double-pile houses feel airless in a way the owners cannot account for.
servicing.heat: A corner or gable-end fireplace with a 30-36 in opening, or none at all: unheated chambers are historically normal and should be said out loud rather than quietly given a register.
servicing.electrical: None historically. In new work, keep the ceiling clear - a chamber ceiling with six recessed cans in it is the fastest way to make a period room read as a reproduction.

style_variation.note: Trim one full grade below the room beneath it. The Georgian graduation is vertical as well as horizontal - the chamber over the parlour has a chair rail and a moulded cornice, the chamber over the hall has a chair rail, the back chambers have neither - and giving every chamber the same trim is the interior equivalent of ungraduated storeys.
Over the hall and the parlour, reached by a winder stair beside the central stack, and warmed by whatever the stack gives up. The unheated chamber is normal here.

Ground-floor chambers are common and correct, and the type's single-pile depth gives every one of them two exterior walls. A tidewater plan drawn double-pile to get more bedrooms has lost the thing the type was for.
At the top of the house the chamber is a state room, with the bed on axis, an alcove or a rail, and trim at the highest grade in the building. Nobody slept in it.
Not a room. The bed stands in the corner of the single heated room, and the loft above holds the children. This is where the type starts.
By 1935 the chamber is gone and the room is a bedroom. Using the word in a mid-century context is an anachronism worth catching.

code.requirement: Emergency escape and rescue opening: 5.7 sq ft net clear (5.0 at grade floor), 24 in minimum clear height, 20 in minimum clear width, sill not more than 44 in above the floor.
code.conflict: A period-correct 12-over-12 sash in a 7 ft 6 in chamber wall has very little room to grow upward before it hits the plate, and the usual fix - widening the opening - produces a squat window that breaks the style's proportion. Take the area out of WIDTH only in a low room, and prefer a casement, which is very often the period-correct answer as well as the code one in first-period and regional work.

sources: Abbott Lowell Cummings, The Framed Houses of Massachusetts Bay 1625-1725 (1979)
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)
